target: यह कमरा उससे ठंडा है।
english: This room is colder than that one.
tip: से glues onto pronouns: उस + से = उससे (usse = than that one). यह कमरा उससे ठंडा है – the 'than that' is one small fused word.

target: यह फ़ोन मेरे पुराने वाले से बेहतर है।
english: This phone is better than my old one.
tip: बेहतर (behtar = better), from Persian, is one of Hindi's few true comparative words: पुराने वाले से बेहतर = better than the old one. Most adjectives rely on से alone.

target: मेरा भाई मुझसे दो साल बड़ा है।
english: My brother is two years older than me.
tip: For people, बड़ा (bada = big) means older: मुझसे दो साल बड़ा (mujhse do saal bada) = two years older than me. छोटा (chhota = small) likewise means younger.

target: सुनील उतना ही अच्छा खेलता है जितना उसका बड़ा भाई।
english: Sunil plays as well as his elder brother.
tip: 'As well as' uses a pair: उतना ही अच्छा... जितना (utna hi achchha... jitna) = 'that much good... as much as'. Hindi spells out both halves of the match.

target: बच्चों की याददाश्त बड़ों से तेज़ होती है।
english: Children's memory is sharper than adults'.
tip: तेज़ (tez) covers fast, sharp, and strong: याददाश्त तेज़ (yaaddaasht tez) = a sharp memory, तेज़ चाकू = a sharp knife, तेज़ धूप = strong sun.

target: पराँठा रोटी से ज़्यादा भरने वाला होता है।
english: Paratha is more filling than roti.
tip: Verb + ने वाला makes 'the ...-ing kind': भरने वाला (bharne vala) = filling, literally 'the one that fills'. Works on nearly any verb.

target: गणित छठी कक्षा से मुश्किल हो जाता है।
english: Math becomes difficult from sixth grade.
tip: This से is 'from', not 'than': छठी कक्षा से (chhathi kaksha se) = from sixth grade onward. से does both jobs; हो जाता है (ho jata hai = becomes) signals a starting point here.

target: सुनीता खाना खाकर बर्तन ख़ुद धो देती है।
english: Sunita washes the dishes herself after eating.
tip: Verb stem + कर = 'after ...ing': खाना खाकर (khana khakar) = after eating. Two syllables replace a whole English clause – 'having eaten, she washes up'.

target: मुझे कॉफ़ी से ज़्यादा चाय पसंद है।
english: I like tea more than coffee.
tip: Liking flips: मुझे चाय पसंद है (mujhe chai pasand hai) = 'to me tea is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे/को (mujhe/ko = to me/to); the tea is the subject.

target: राजेश के हिसाब से यह आइडिया बिल्कुल नया है।
english: According to Rajesh, this idea is completely new.
tip: के हिसाब से (ke hisaab se) = 'by the account of' = according to: राजेश के हिसाब से = according to Rajesh. हिसाब (hisaab) means account or calculation.

target: नई गाड़ी पुरानी से कम पेट्रोल पीती है।
english: The new car uses less petrol than the old one.
tip: Vehicles drink fuel: कम पेट्रोल पीती है (kam petrol peeti hai) = uses less petrol, literally 'drinks less'. पीना (peena) also covers smoking – सिगरेट पीना.

target: व्रत के दिन हम साबूदाने की खिचड़ी खाते हैं।
english: On fasting days we eat sago khichdi.
tip: साबूदाने की खिचड़ी (sabudane ki khichdi = sago khichdi) is the classic व्रत (vrat = fast) meal – grains are avoided on fasting days, and sago isn't a grain.

target: दीवाली पर हम घर में अलग-अलग मिठाइयाँ बनाते हैं।
english: On Diwali we make different sweets at home.
tip: Doubling a word spreads it out: अलग-अलग (alag-alag = different-different) = all kinds of. Hindi repeats where English says 'various' or 'each'.

target: हमने आज पहली बार तंदूरी रोटी घर पर बनाई।
english: Today we made tandoori roti at home for the first time.
tip: With हमने (humne = we), the verb agrees with the thing made: बनाई (banai) is feminine because रोटी (roti) is – 'made' matches the roti, not us.

target: मेरे मामा का बेटा मेरा सबसे अच्छा दोस्त भी है।
english: My maternal uncle's son is also my best friend.
tip: There is no word for cousin – you describe the route: मामा का बेटा (mama ka beta) = mother's brother's son. Cousins are often simply called भाई (bhai = brother).

target: करोड़ों लोग हर साल इस धार्मिक जगह पर आते हैं।
english: Crores of people come to this pilgrimage site every year.
tip: करोड़ों (karodon = crores of): Hindi counts big numbers as लाख (lakh = 100,000) and करोड़ (crore = 10 million) – 'million' barely exists in daily speech.

target: रानी की कोशिश सफल रही, यानी उसकी मेहनत रंग लाई।
english: Rani's effort was successful, that is her hard work paid off.
tip: मेहनत रंग लाई (mehnat rang layi) = 'the hard work brought color' – the set idiom for effort paying off. In Hindi, success shows up as color.

target: गर्मियाँ तो सर्दियों से लंबी होती ही हैं।
english: Summers are longer than winters.
tip: ही (hi) stresses the word before it: होती ही हैं (hoti hi hain) = simply ARE longer. This tiny word does what English does with voice stress or 'indeed'.

target: यह इलाके का सबसे अच्छा डॉक्टर है।
english: This is the best doctor in the area.
tip: 'Best in the area' becomes 'the area's best': इलाके का सबसे अच्छा डॉक्टर (ilake ka sabse achchha doctor) – Hindi reaches for का (ka = of) where English says 'in'.

target: तिल के लड्डू मकर संक्रांति पर बनते हैं।
english: Sesame laddoos are made on Makar Sankranti.
tip: बनते हैं (bante hain) = 'get made': बनना (banna) is a verb meaning 'to be made', so लड्डू बनते हैं says laddoos get made with no doer mentioned.

target: बिल मेरी उम्मीद से ज़्यादा आया।
english: The bill came to more than I expected.
tip: से can compare against an idea: उम्मीद से ज़्यादा (ummeed se zyada) = 'more than hope' = more than expected. Any noun can serve as the measuring stick.

target: ताऊ जी पहलवानी किया करते थे।
english: Uncle used to practice wrestling.
tip: किया करते थे (kiya karte the) adds 'made a habit of it' – the verb's -या (-ya) form + करना (karna) is a step more nostalgic than plain करते थे (karte the). Common when reminiscing.

target: दादी हर रात लोरियाँ सुनाती थीं।
english: Grandmother used to sing lullabies every night.
tip: One respected grandmother, plural verb: दादी (dadi) takes सुनाती थीं (sunati theen), not थी (thi). Elders and parents get grammatical plural as respect.

target: हमारी नानी लोरी गाकर सुलाती थीं।
english: Our grandmother used to put us to sleep by singing lullabies.
tip: गाकर (gaakar = having sung) – adding -कर (-kar) to a verb means 'by/after doing it', chaining actions with no word for 'and': sang, and so put us to sleep.

target: चाचा जी शतरंज बहुत अच्छी खेलते थे।
english: Uncle used to play chess very well.
tip: 'Played chess well' – well is the adjective अच्छी (achchhi), agreeing with feminine शतरंज (shatranj). Manner words often match the object's gender.

target: वह रोज़ शाम को बाँसुरी बजाता था।
english: He used to play the flute every evening.
tip: English 'play' splits in Hindi: instruments take बजाना (bajana = make sound) – बाँसुरी बजाता था (bansuri bajata tha). Games take खेलना (khelna). Never swap them.

target: कुएँ का पानी बहुत मीठा होता था।
english: The well water used to be very sweet.
tip: मीठा होता था (meetha hota tha) = 'used to be sweet, as a rule'. Plain था (tha) would pin it to one occasion – होता था signals a general truth back then.

target: पहले मैं रोज़ सुबह जिम जाता था।
english: I used to go to the gym every morning.
tip: जाता था (jata tha), the -ता (-ta) form + था (tha), is Hindi's plain 'used to' – no extra word needed. पहले (pahle = earlier) just sets the scene.

target: हम साइकिल से पाँच किलोमीटर दूर स्कूल जाते थे।
english: We used to bike to a school five kilometers away.
tip: साइकिल से (cycle se) = by bike – से (se) is the all-purpose 'by/with/from': vehicles, tools, and starting points all use the same little word.

target: बारिश में हम काग़ज़ की नावें बनाते थे।
english: We used to make paper boats in the rain.
tip: काग़ज़ की नावें (kagaz ki naavein) = boats of paper – की/का (ki/ka) marks material, and it agrees with the thing made: feminine की for the boats, not the paper.
